extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in humor, social dynamics, or linguistics
extracted.subtask_description: Describes what counts as an in-joke/inside joke: its defining features, variants (e.g., callbacks), social functions, typical structure, and examples. Useful for identifying, analyzing, or producing humor that is only understood by a particular in-group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: in-joke/inside joke
rubrics_metrics.description: An in-joke, also known as an inside joke or a private joke, is a joke with humour that is understandable only to members of an in-group; that is, people who are in a particular social group, occupation, or other community of shared interest. It is, therefore, an esoteric joke, only humorous to those who are aware of the circumstances behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on shared background knowledge or circumstances: if the audience lacks that knowledge, the joke will not be funny to them. The page uses the term 'esoteric' to highlight exclusivity of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference-based punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, inside jokes use a reference in the punchline to imply that which is associated with the reference. Often, this reference refers to the punchline of another joke which was already heard by the in-group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful in-jokes rely on a reference that carries meaning only for the in-group; producing them requires embedding or alluding to that shared referent. The page gives the general structural principle rather than formal steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback variant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the in-group only includes people which heard the previous portion of a comedic set, the type of inside joke is known as a callback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use callbacks to reward audience members who followed earlier material; callbacks assume immediate prior knowledge rather than long-standing shared context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and scope (clique to profession)
rubrics_metrics.description: In-jokes may exist within a small social clique, such as a group of friends, or extend to an entire profession or other relatively large group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or creating an in-joke, consider intended audience scale — intimacy of the reference differs if targeted at a handful of friends versus an entire occupational community (e.g., mathematical jokes, military humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function: community-building and exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An in-joke may be used to build community, sometimes at the expense of outsiders. Part of the power of an in-joke is that its audience knows that many do not understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the dual social effect: inclusion for the in-group and exclusion or alienation for outsiders. This is a deliberate social dynamic often exploited in group bonding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical framing — cryptic allusions as selective triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: In-jokes are cryptic allusions to shared common ground that act as selective triggers; only those who share that common ground are able to respond appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an in-joke by whether it functions as a selective trigger: does it reliably elicit the intended response from those possessing the shared knowledge while leaving others unresponsive?

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtext usage and tacit apology to newcomers
rubrics_metrics.description: An in-joke can also be used as a subtext, where people in the know may find humor in something not explicitly spoken. They may even apologize for doing so to a rookie, directly or indirectly stating that what they were laughing at was an in-joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using in-jokes as subtext, be aware of social etiquette: groups sometimes acknowledge and soften exclusion by apologizing or signaling that the laughter was based on insider knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-knowledge requirement (example: pun on specialized concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals not familiar with the mathematical result Zorn's lemma are unlikely to understand the joke. The provided example: 'Q: What's yellow and equivalent to the axiom of choice? A: Zorn's lemon.' — a pun on the name of this result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that in-jokes often depend on specialized domain knowledge (here, mathematics). Use concrete examples to test whether a reference will be accessible to the intended in-group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/ethnic/religious in-jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethnic or religious groups may also have in-jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of sensitivity: in-jokes tied to ethnicity or religion can reinforce in-group identity but also risk offense or stereotyping when exposed to outsiders.
